meta.title: Checkouts blocked for 94 minutes
meta.subtitle: A rate-limit config set burst limits to zero for tenants without custom limits, stopping checkouts for 94 minutes

overview.takeaway: The config removed the burst fallback, blocking each window's first request for tenants without custom limits until rollback.

timeline.sub: Times are Pacific; hover over a time to see UTC.
timeline.takeaway: The monitor fired after nineteen minutes; responders read the limiter config another 75 minutes later.

causes.takeaway: The rollout spread refusals from the missing fallback everywhere at once. Monitor delays prolonged the incident.

impact.takeaway: Tenants without custom limits faced checkout failures for 94 minutes; 11 400 confirmations were late. Orders weren't lost.

resolution.takeaway: Rollback stopped refusals within a minute; that afternoon's fix restored the fallback with a test for missing defaults.

lessons.takeaway: The rollback and shared channel worked; the open dashboard directed responders toward the wrong initial hypothesis.

recognize.takeaway: Checkout 5xx spikes with 429 upstream error bodies point to the edge limiter, not the payment provider.

actions.takeaway: The fix and monitor update shipped; staged rollout work remains open to contain other config defects.

unknowns.takeaway: The true late-confirmation count and why the canary shared the config remain two unanswered questions.

causes: What was the root cause, and what merely triggered it?
actions: What is still open, and who owns it?

meta.canonical: This file is the canonical retro. Snapshots of the evidence live under evidence/; prose that does not fit structure lives in NOTES.md; incident-retro.html renders from this file.

summary.text: A config push to the checkout edge shipped a rate-limit profile with a zero default for missing per-tenant burst overrides. That zero burst default rejected the first request in each window for every tenant without an override, returning a 429 that the checkout API surfaced as a 5xx. The 5xx monitor's long window delayed detection. A rollback stopped the failures; a burst floor and config test prevent recurrence.
summary.p: A settings change blocked many checkout requests. A monitor caught the failures, we reversed the change, and a minimum request allowance now prevents the same failure.

windows.text: For tenants without a burst override, the first checkout request in every limiter window failed.
The retry queue replayed failed checkouts at a capped rate, so their confirmations arrived late.

timeline.text: The release bot pushed `rate-limit-v7` to the checkout edge in every region at once.
The first failed checkout appeared in the request log, but no one was watching it yet.
Support posted two customer reports in the incident channel.
The incident was declared; Priya took command and paged the platform on-call.
The payment provider was suspected; its status page was green and its latency was flat.
Tom found `429 upstream` in the error bodies and suspected the edge rate limiter.
The limiter config comparison showed that `us-west` and the canary region both carried `rate-limit-v7`.
The config check confirmed that `rate-limit-v7` set per-tenant burst to zero for tenants without an override.
On-call rolled the edge back to `rate-limit-v6`; the error rate dropped within a minute.
The retry queue replayed the failed checkouts at its capped rate.
The fix shipped with a burst floor of one and a config schema test.
The retry queue drained, and confirmation latency returned to baseline.
The monitor stayed green for an hour, and the all clear was posted to the incident channel.
The retro meeting was held, and action items were assigned.

impact.text: Tenants without a burst override could not complete a checkout during the first window (W1); the limiter refused their first request in every limiter window. Tenants with an override were unaffected. Through the second window (W2), confirmations for replayed checkouts arrived late.
impact.p: Most customers could not check out for a while. Their retried orders confirmed late afterward. Customers with custom limits were unaffected.

teams.text: Owned the failing endpoint and retry queue and ran the replay.
Owns the edge limiter and the config pipeline that shipped `rate-limit-v7`.

causes.t: The limiter treated a missing burst override as zero
causes.text: `rate-limit-v7` replaced the hardcoded per-tenant burst default with an override map. A tenant missing from the map received the Go struct field's zero value. Its first request in every window exceeded a burst of zero and received a 429. The notebook's second chart shows 429s rising only for tenants without an override (T7).
causes.p: The new settings lacked a fallback, so customers without custom settings got a limit of zero and their requests were refused.

code.caption: The fix restores the v6 guard that v7 removed, using a floor of one (C1).

causes.t: The config push rolled to every region at once
causes.text: The edge config pipeline has no canary stage, so `rate-limit-v7` reached every region in one step (T1). A staged rollout would have limited the outage to the canary region and shown the 429s before the monitor fired.
causes.p: The change reached every region at once instead of one region first, so a small failure could not warn of a larger one.

causes.t: The 5xx monitor evaluated over a long window
causes.text: `Checkout 5xx rate` averages over a fifteen-minute window and requires a full window before firing, so it alerted well after the first failures (T3). Support received customer reports before the alert reached on-call.
causes.p: The alarm required a long stretch of failures before firing, so people noticed the problem before the alert.

resolution.text: On-call rolled the edge back to `rate-limit-v6` (T10), stopping the 429s immediately. The checkout team replayed failed orders from the retry queue at its capped rate through the second window (W2). The fix landed that afternoon with a burst floor of one and a schema test that rejects profiles with an empty override map.
resolution.p: We reversed the change, retried the failed orders, and then shipped a fix with a minimum request allowance and a test.

detection.text: The `Checkout 5xx rate` monitor caught the incident (slow monitor window) only after its window filled. Support received two customer reports first. The monitor now evaluates over five minutes and pages on the first breach.
detection.p: Customers reported the problem before the automatic alarm caught it. The alarm now responds sooner.

decisions.t: Roll back the edge rather than patch the profile
decisions.why: The previous profile was ready in the pipeline. Rolling back took one step with a known result; patching forward required a build and review that could not be shortened.
decisions.alternatives: Editing each region's override map by hand would have left three regions in three different states.

decisions.t: Replay the retry queue without raising its rate cap
decisions.why: The payment provider applies rate limits per merchant. A burst of replays risked a second incident on a dependency outside our control.
decisions.alternatives: Raise the replay cap to drain the queue in minutes, with the risk of exceeding the provider's unknown limit.

decisions.t: Ship the burst floor that day rather than wait for the staged rollout
decisions.why: The burst floor needed three lines and a test; the staged rollout required weeks of pipeline work. Leaving this class of failure unresolved over a weekend posed more risk than shipping the floor.
decisions.alternatives: Wait to ship the burst floor until the staged rollout was ready.

hypotheses.t: The payment provider was failing requests or rate-limiting them
hypotheses.exonerated: The provider's status page was green, and its p99 latency stayed flat throughout the window. Our error bodies contained 429 upstream, which the provider never sends.

hypotheses.t: The canary region ran an older, healthy config
hypotheses.exonerated: The comparison found the same `rate-limit-v7` profile in both regions. The pipeline has no canary stage to hold one region back.

hypotheses.t: A Redis eviction removed the limiter's per-tenant counters
hypotheses.exonerated: Eviction counters stayed flat, and memory remained well below the limit throughout the window. Refusals followed the override map rather than memory pressure.

hypotheses.t: The config build truncated the override map
hypotheses.exonerated: The build emitted every map entry. The fall-through came from the missing default, which the schema test now checks for.

recognize.signal: Checkout 5xx errors rise while the payment provider's dashboard stays flat
recognize.means: Our system rejects the request between the edge and the API; the dependency is not the source.
recognize.do: Read an error body before checking the provider's dashboard.

recognize.signal: A 5xx response with `429 upstream` in its error body
recognize.means: The edge limiter refuses the request, and the API reports that refusal as a server error.
recognize.do: In every region, compare the live limiter profile with the previous one.

recognize.signal: A tenant's first request fails in each window, but later requests succeed
recognize.means: The burst allowance is at or near zero; the sustained-rate limit is not the cause.
recognize.do: Compare the burst values of a failing tenant and an unaffected tenant.

recognize.signal: A config push reached every region within one minute
recognize.means: The canary did not receive the profile first, so the bad profile is already in every region.
recognize.do: Roll back first. The previous profile is ready in the pipeline.

unknowns.q: How many confirmations did customers receive late?
unknowns.why: The late-confirmation count includes every order whose confirmation was sent after the session ended. The session log supports only an estimate, and the mail provider's delivery log had expired.

unknowns.q: Why does the canary region receive the same config push as production?
unknowns.why: The pipeline was designed with a canary stage. The review did not establish when or why it stopped holding one region back.

unknowns.q: With the shorter window, would the monitor have fired before the first customer report?
unknowns.why: The five-minute window is faster in theory. The retained error-rate data from the first minutes is too coarse to establish when the monitor would have fired.

glossary.def: A tenant's allowance for requests sent at once, before the sustained rate applies. A burst of zero refuses the first request.
A config profile's per-tenant limiter settings. Tenants missing from the map use the profile's default.
One versioned config for the edge limiter, such as `rate-limit-v7`, shipped to every region as a unit.
The layer in front of the checkout API that applies rate limits before requests reach application code.
A durable queue that stores failed checkouts for replay once the cause is removed.
The region meant to receive changes first. Edge config changes currently reach it at the same time as every other region.

actions.t: Add a burst floor and test the config schema
actions.note: The burst floor and config schema test are complete.

actions.t: Shorten the checkout 5xx monitor's evaluation window
actions.note: The shorter checkout monitor window is in place.

actions.t: Roll out edge config changes region by region
actions.note: The regional rollout is still in progress.
The limiter runbook remains to be written.

actions.t: Add a synthetic checkout every minute
actions.note: The faster checkout monitor covers the same detection gap at no extra cost.

well.text: The rollback worked the first time. The edge config pipeline keeps the previous profile ready to use.
Support and on-call shared one channel, so responders received customer reports unfiltered.

wrong.text: The first hypothesis focused on the payment provider because its dashboard was open. The error bodies already pointed to the cause.
The config schema had no way to require a key, so the struct default behavior shipped without a test.

lucky.text: The retry queue retained every failed checkout, so the orders were delayed and none were lost.

images.alt: Error rate chart with the rollback marked
images.caption: The error rate fell within a minute of the rollback (W1).

notes.md: The retry queue held 3 180 failed checkouts at rollback. Replay stayed within the queue's rate cap, avoiding a burst at the payment provider; every order confirmed by the end of the slow retry drain (W2). The late confirmation count includes every order whose confirmation email was sent after the customer's session ended. The count is an estimate from the session log.[^1]

footnotes.b: Session end is the customer's last browser request. A customer who left the tab open counts as not late.
